svg.aria-label: Diagram: what the AWS AI/ML skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS adds, what it replaces, and what its capability list implies about permissions and cost. AWS states that a coding agent can select, train, optimize and deploy models on Amazon SageMaker AI while working across the rest of the AWS environment in a single natural-language workflow, and that the AWS AI/ML skill is now a core skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS so it works alongside the toolkit's other AWS skills such as EC2 and Bedrock. The skill is pre-installed into SageMaker Studio JupyterLab for use with Kiro or another coding agent, and can otherwise be installed from the Agent Toolkit for AWS on GitHub. The capability areas are inference optimization, meaning optimizing deployed models for latency, throughput and cost; model customization, meaning end-to-end guided fine-tuning workflows from use case definition through training, evaluation and deployment; serverful training for both traditional machine learning and generative AI; MLflow for experiment tracking and model lifecycle management; JumpStart model deployment and model recommendations, covering deployment of pre-built JumpStart models and guided recommendations on the right model for a use case; and processing jobs, covering data preparation and ETL on managed compute. The first of the two statements that matter more than the capability list is a deprecation carried in the middle of the announcement: the toolkit is now the single, supported integration point, replacing the previous AWS Labs skills and plugins, with a consistent and easy install and update path. Anyone with AWS Labs skills or plugins wired into a workflow is therefore on a replaced path, and that is a migration notice rather than a feature. The second is the pricing line, which should be read as an architecture statement rather than a cost note: the skill is available at no additional charge and you pay only for the AWS resources your agents use. That sentence establishes that the agent provisions billable infrastructure, because something that only read configuration would generate no resource charges at all. The capability list reinforces it, since training, deploying, running processing jobs and optimising endpoints are all mutating operations on managed compute, so the list should be read as a permission requirement rather than a feature list. The practical consequence is that the permission boundary becomes the design question the announcement does not address: the agent acts with whatever credentials the environment gives it, so in SageMaker Studio JupyterLab, where the skill arrives pre-installed, that is the Studio execution role, and that role was scoped for a human working deliberately rather than for an agent acting on a sentence. Security implications follow from the capabilities: an agent that can run processing jobs for data preparation and ETL on managed compute is an agent that reads the customer's data, and an agent that can perform end-to-end guided fine-tuning is one that can train a model on it, so the execution role's data access is now exercised by something acting on an instruction in English. Three questions are worth settling before installation rather than after: which role the agent assumes, what that role can reach, and what the audit trail shows, since CloudTrail records the role and the API call but not the sentence that caused it, so attribution stops at the role. On cost, the skill itself carries no additional charge but training jobs and inference endpoints are among the few AWS costs that accumulate quickly, and an endpoint left deployed bills continuously whether or not anyone calls it, while an agent is good at creating resources and has no particular instinct for tidying up, so a conversation that deploys three JumpStart models to compare them leaves three endpoints running unless somebody removes them. Recommended controls are therefore an execution role scoped to the specific SageMaker actions the work needs rather than a broad managed policy, a budget with an alert configured before anyone deploys a model, a check of whether Studio JupyterLab users already have the skill present by default, an inventory of existing AWS Labs skills and plugins to plan the move while it is unforced, a CloudTrail review of endpoints and training jobs created by the execution role, and an agreed teardown habit.
svg.title: Six mutating capability areas, an execution role scoped for a human, and a deprecation in the middle
svg.text: Read the capability list as a permission list.
The AWS AI/ML skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS — an agent that trains, deploys and bills.
Six capability areas — every one of them a mutation on managed compute
Inference optimization — “optimize deployed models for latency, throughput, and cost”
Model customization — “end-to-end guided fine-tuning workflows”, use case through deployment
Serverful training · MLflow · JumpStart deployment + recommendations
Processing jobs — “data preparation and ETL on managed compute” — i.e. it reads your data
Train, deploy, optimise, process. None of these is a read.
Sentence 1 — a deprecation, mid-paragraph
“The toolkit is now the single, supported

text.tspan: integration point, replacing the previous AWS

svg.text: Labs skills and plugins”
No date, no removal notice. Move while it is a choice
rather than an emergency.
Sentence 2 — a pricing note that is an architecture fact
“available at no additional charge; you pay only for
the AWS resources your agents use”
Something that only read config would generate no
resource charges at all.
So: the agent provisions billable infrastructure.
Which makes the permission boundary the design question the announcement does not address
The agent acts with whatever credentials its environment gives it. The skill is “pre-installed into SageMaker
Studio JupyterLab” — so that is the Studio execution role, scoped for a person working deliberately,
now backing an agent acting on a sentence. And it may already be there without a decision.
Three questions, before the install
1 · Which role does it assume?
2 · What can that role reach?
3 · What does the audit trail show?
CloudTrail records the role and the call, not the prompt.
The cost shape to guard
Training jobs and inference endpoints run to real money
fast, and an endpoint bills whether or not it is called.
An agent creates readily and tidies up only if asked.
“Compare three JumpStart models” = three live endpoints.
The genuine win is consolidation: “a consistent and easy install and update path”, and one answer to “which integration is supported”.
Plus cross-service reach — “alongside the toolkit’s other AWS skills like EC2, Bedrock, and more” — because a deployment is never only a deployment.
Budget first, scope the role second, experiment third.
Attribution stops at the role: the log answers which credential, and the question has become which instruction.
Same gap as the resource-share post: the record names the principal, not the identity that used it.
